item_title: News On Japan reported (Nov 23) that the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell more than 10% below their previous peaks, entering correction territory
mechanism: A broad equity drawdown raises the cost of new equity and narrows the window for listings, which pushes AI builders further toward debt.

scenarios.direction: The correction deepens, listings and large equity raises are deferred, and AI builders lean harder on bonds and private credit.
scenarios.why: Equity issuance depends on buyers willing to pay up, and a falling market removes that, so funding gaps are filled with borrowing on whatever terms are open.
scenarios.precedent: After the dot-com peak in March 2000, US IPO issuance fell sharply through 2001 and 2002 while telecom borrowers carried heavy debt.

scenarios.direction: The correction proves short, equity windows reopen, and the financing mix changes little.
scenarios.why: Lower Treasury yields, which the article reported, reduce the base rate for borrowers and can support risk assets once volatility fades.
scenarios.precedent: The S&P 500 fell about 20% into December 2018 and had recovered its high by April 2019.

scenarios.direction: Credit markets reprice AI borrowers alongside equities, so debt costs rise as equity value falls.
scenarios.why: Many AI borrowers' creditworthiness rests on the same expected cash flows that equity investors are now questioning.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, predates this selloff and carries no reading on equity-market drawdowns or AI financing conditions.

item_title: A paper by Gabriel Borrageiro, posted to arXiv on Nov 15, states that CME and ICE futures on compute rental rates reference published short-dated rental rates, while most operator revenue comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed
mechanism: Futures that settle on published short-dated rental rates may not track revenue earned on private multi-year contracts, leaving operators and lenders with a hedge that fits poorly.

scenarios.direction: Contract prices become more visible or index-linked, and the listed futures track operator revenue more closely.
scenarios.why: Traded contracts need a reference price, and long-term contracts tend to adopt it once it exists and is trusted.
scenarios.precedent: Long-term oil supply contracts came to be priced off the Brent and WTI benchmarks after futures on them began trading in the 1980s.

scenarios.direction: Short-dated rental rates fall while contracted revenue holds, and a hedge pays out on a move the operators' revenue never felt.
scenarios.why: The paper states the contracts reference short-dated rates, while most revenue sits in private multi-year contracts that do not reprice with them.

scenarios.direction: Lenders keep relying on private contract terms and prepayment clauses rather than on listed hedges, so the risk stays inside credit agreements.
scenarios.why: The paper states that contract prices are largely undisclosed, which limits what outsiders can hedge or price.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, covers rates, Treasury long-end conditions and fund flows but carries no reading on compute-market hedging or AI borrowing.

item_title: WIRED reported (Nov 23) that the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent in the week before Nov 23, in part due to Nvidia's struggles, the index's biggest decline since March 2020
mechanism: Nvidia's heavy weight in the Nasdaq lets news about its chief executive move the index, so the week's fall and Monday's rebound may track one stock's governance news.

scenarios.direction: The rebound holds and the index recovers much of the week's loss as Nvidia's weight lifts it.
scenarios.why: A stock carrying a large share of an index passes its own gains through to the index, so a lasting recovery in Nvidia would repair the index with it.
scenarios.precedent: The Nasdaq Composite fell about 30% from February to March 2020 and was back at a record high by June 2020.

scenarios.direction: Monday's jump proves a one-day relief and selling resumes as the investigations and hearings continue.
scenarios.why: The board's reversal removes one uncertainty but not the open inquiries, the Dec 1 to Dec 3 hearings or the Entity List action reported against Megaspeed.
scenarios.precedent: The Nasdaq Composite fell about 78% from March 2000 to October 2002, with sharp rallies along the way.

scenarios.direction: The index stays tied to one company's news, so a further governance headline moves it again in either direction.
scenarios.why: When a single stock's weight is large, index moves follow that stock's news more than the broad market.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, predates this move and carries no reading on index concentration or AI-stock drawdowns.

item_title: Crunchbase News reported that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion on their last reported valuations, and that its new Current Valuation Model puts that figure closer to $11 trillion
mechanism: A listing replaces a private estimate with a market price, so a board of private valuations can fall when its largest member lists and is priced by traders instead.

scenarios.direction: Other large private AI companies list, and their private marks are reset to market prices that differ from their last rounds.
scenarios.why: Each listing exchanges a negotiated round price for a daily market price, and the two need not agree, so the board's total moves with the gap.
scenarios.precedent: WeWork was valued at $47 billion in a January 2019 private round and was marked far lower in September 2019 when its IPO was pulled.

scenarios.direction: Private marks keep rising on the model's estimates while public prices for listed AI companies fall.
scenarios.why: The Current Valuation Model estimates a higher figure than last rounds, and nothing in it forces a mark to follow a public selloff until a company lists.

scenarios.direction: New rounds price close to the model's estimates, so the gap between last rounds and current values closes through up-rounds.
scenarios.why: Sierra's reported $30 billion round sits near the model's $31.5 billion estimate, which is one data point for rounds meeting the model.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, predates the Anthropic IPO and carries no reading on private-market valuations.

item_title: TechCrunch reported (Nov 24) that Anthropic's stock fell below its $83 IPO price, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday's close
mechanism: An IPO price is the level underwriters set, so trading below it shows buyers valuing the shares under that mark, which private holders and later issuers can use as a reference.

scenarios.direction: Shares recover above $83 as early trading settles and the first results arrive.
scenarios.why: Early IPO trading is volatile, and a price below the offer can recover once supply from early sellers has been absorbed.
scenarios.precedent: Facebook priced at $38 in May 2012, fell to about $31 within days, and traded above $38 again in August 2013.

scenarios.direction: The slide continues and marks on private AI companies and plans for other listings come under pressure.
scenarios.why: A public price under the offer gives private investors and later issuers a fresh market reference that sits below the last round's price.
scenarios.precedent: Uber priced at $45 in May 2019, closed its first day at $41.57 and ended 2019 near $30.

scenarios.direction: Shares hold near $83 for a time before the next move.
scenarios.why: Underwriters can buy shares in the market to support the price near the offer, which can keep trading close to it for a while.
scenarios.precedent: Facebook's underwriters bought shares at $38 on its first day of trading in May 2012 to hold the price at the offer.

context_note: The standing snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, predates the Anthropic IPO and carries no reading on public pricing of AI labs.

item_title: Applied Digital stated in a press release furnished with its Form 8-K that on Nov 23 it entered into a new 18-year lease with an unnamed tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler for 150 MW of critical IT capacity, providing about $5.4 billion in base-term contracted revenue, or about $12.7 billion if all renewal options are exercised over a 33-year total term
mechanism: A lease from an investment-grade tenant gives the developer contracted revenue to borrow against, so project debt rests on the tenant's credit more than on the developer's.

scenarios.direction: Project financing is raised against the lease on the path the chief financial officer described.
scenarios.why: Lenders price against the tenant's credit and the lease term, so a long lease from a highly rated tenant supports borrowing sized to the contracted payments.
scenarios.precedent: CoreWeave raised a $2.3 billion debt facility in 2023 collateralized by its Nvidia GPUs and customer contracts.

scenarios.direction: Debt sized to the lease carries more risk than the tenant's name implies if construction runs late.
scenarios.why: Contracted payments usually start when capacity is delivered, so delays or cost overruns fall on the developer and its lenders until then.

context_note: The standing snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, predates this lease and carries no reading on lease-backed data-center borrowing.
